maths_errors.text: Two quantities are in direct proportion when they increase and decrease together at the same rate — doubling one doubles the other.
maths_errors.correction: Direct proportion does not mean the quantities change 'at the same rate'. In the lesson's own example, y = 3x, y increases 3 times as fast as x. The correct statement is that y is always the same multiple of x (y = kx). This means y/x is constant, and if one is multiplied by a number, the other is multiplied by the same number.

maths_errors.text: Direct proportion: as x increases, y increases (y = kx). Inverse proportion: as x increases, y decreases (y = k/x).
maths_errors.correction: This is presented as the way to tell the two apart, but it is not a correct test. y = x + 5 increases with x but is not direct proportion. y = 10 − x decreases as x increases but is not inverse proportion. The defining tests are: y/x is constant (direct), or xy is constant (inverse). Equivalently, multiplying x by a number multiplies y by that number (direct) or divides y by it (inverse).

false_mistakes.text: Using an additive method rather than finding k — e.g. for y = kx with x going from 4 to 7 (an increase of 3), adding 3 × (some value) to y instead of finding k = y/x and calculating y = k × 7.
false_mistakes.why: For y = kx, an increase of 3 in x always gives an increase of 3k in y. So 'adding 3 × (some value) to y' is a valid method when the value is k, the amount y goes up per 1 unit of x. The described method is not in itself a mistake. The real error is adding 3 directly to y, or adding a multiple that is not k, and the item does not say that. The correction's claim 'Proportion is always multiplicative' therefore overstates the case.
false_mistakes.mistaken_method_gives: With k as the value: if x = 4, y = 12 (k = 3), then y = 12 + 3 × 3 = 21. This equals 3 × 7 = 21, the correct answer.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: understand and use proportion as equality of ratios
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson only says 'The ratio y/x is the same for every pair of values' and gives no teaching on proportion as equality of ratios. It does not show, for example, 5 : 15 = 8 : y, or a scale-factor or unitary method that solves a proportion without first finding k.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: solve problems involving direct and inverse proportion, including graphical and algebraic representations
missing_spec_content.why: Graphical representations are not taught at all. Nothing explains that direct proportion gives a straight line through the origin with gradient k, or that inverse proportion gives the curve y = k/x. Problem solving in context is also not taught. Recipes, currency and speed are named in slides[0].body, but no contextual problem is worked.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: understand that X is inversely proportional to Y is equivalent to X is proportional to 1/Y
missing_spec_content.why: slides[1].formula writes 'Inverse: y = k/x (or y ∝ 1/x)' but never explains why 'inversely proportional to x' means the same as 'proportional to 1/x'.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: interpret equations that describe direct and inverse proportion
missing_spec_content.why: No part of the lesson asks the student to read a given equation, such as y = 7/x or P = 2.5t, and decide which kind of proportion it shows, or what k means in context.

cases_not_modelled.why: The only worked example is direct proportion. The student never sees k = xy found and used.

cases_not_modelled.case: proportion to a power or root (e.g. y ∝ x², y ∝ x³, y ∝ √x)
cases_not_modelled.why: y ∝ x² appears only in a common-mistake item. No worked example shows it.

cases_not_modelled.case: inverse proportion to a power (e.g. y ∝ 1/x²)
cases_not_modelled.why: 'y = k/xⁿ' is listed in slides[1].formula but never modelled.

cases_not_modelled.case: finding x given y (working backwards from the equation)
cases_not_modelled.why: The worked example only finds y from x.

cases_not_modelled.case: contextual word problem (e.g. recipe scaling, currency, workers and time)
cases_not_modelled.why: Contexts are named in slides[0].body but none is worked.

cases_not_modelled.case: graphical proportion (reading k from, or recognising, a graph)
solving using equality of ratios or the unitary method without k
cases_not_modelled.why: Every method shown goes through the constant k.

cases_not_modelled.case: constructing and stating the equation as the final answer (e.g. 'find a formula for y in terms of x')
cases_not_modelled.why: This Higher requirement is only implied by the result 'k = 3, so y = 3x'. It is not shown as a question type in its own right.

density.text: Direct: y = kx (or y ∝ x) | Inverse: y = k/x (or y ∝ 1/x) | Other: y = kxⁿ or y = k/xⁿ
density.why: Six relationships are packed into one line separated by bars. The symbol ∝ and the notation xⁿ are used without saying what they mean ('is proportional to'; 'x to the power n').

density.text: k is the constant of proportionality — it stays the same for all pairs of x and y values in the relationship. To find k: substitute a given pair of values into the equation and solve. For direct proportion (y = kx), k = y ÷ x. For inverse proportion (y = k/x), k = y × x. Once k is known, the equation gives any other value. For proportion involving powers (e.g. y ∝ x², write y = kx² and find k the same way.
density.why: This is one paragraph carrying the definition of k, the general method, two rearrangements and an extension to powers. It does not explain why k = y × x for inverse proportion (multiplying both sides of y = k/x by x).

density.text: Confusing direct and inverse proportion — e.g. for y ∝ 1/x, writing y = kx (direct) instead of y = k/x, then getting k = y/x instead of k = yx.
density.why: One sentence holds two linked errors and four expressions. There are no numbers to make it concrete.

density.text: adding 3 × (some value) to y instead of finding k = y/x and calculating y = k × 7
density.why: 'Some value' is vague, so a first-time learner cannot tell what the wrong method actually is. No y-value is given to try it with.

density.text: Square x first: y = kx² → k = y ÷ x² = 36 ÷ 3² = 36 ÷ 9 = 4. Then y = 4x².
density.why: This is a chain with an arrow and four equals signs on one line. The rearrangement from y = kx² to k = y ÷ x² is not explained.
